content: The March 2021 edition of this review demonstrated that thoracic imaging, particularly computed tomography (CT), is highly sensitive and moderately specific for diagnosing COVID-19 pneumonia. This updated review aims to reassess the diagnostic accuracy of thoracic imaging in individuals suspected of having COVID-19, evaluate the rate of positive imaging findings in cases where initial reverse transcriptase polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) results were negative but later turned positive, and assess the accuracy of thoracic imaging in screening asymptomatic individuals. Additionally, the review sought to explore how varying thresholds for test positivity might influence diagnostic accuracy. The search for relevant studies was conducted across multiple databases, including the COVID-19 Living Evidence Database, the Cochrane COVID-19 Study Register, and others, up to February 17, 2021. No language restrictions were applied. The review included diagnostic accuracy studies involving participants of any age suspected of having COVID-19. Eligible studies assessed chest CT, chest X-ray, or lung ultrasound for diagnosing COVID-19, used RT-PCR as the reference standard, and reported or provided data to calculate test accuracy. Studies using imaging as part of the reference standard or excluding participants with normal imaging results were excluded. A total of 98 studies were included in the review. Of these, 94 studies evaluated the diagnostic accuracy of thoracic imaging in suspected COVID-19 cases, 8 studies assessed the rate of positive imaging findings in individuals with initially negative RT-PCR results who later tested positive, and 10 studies evaluated the accuracy of imaging in asymptomatic individuals. Across all studies, the risk of bias was high or unclear in a significant proportion of studies, particularly regarding participant selection, reference standards, index tests, and flow/timing. Concerns about the applicability of the evidence were also noted in a smaller subset of studies. For individuals suspected of having COVID-19, 94 studies were analyzed. Among these, 87 studies evaluated a single imaging modality, while 7 studies assessed two modalities. All studies used RT-PCR, either alone or in combination with clinical criteria, as the reference standard. For chest CT (69 studies, 28,285 participants, 51% confirmed cases), sensitivity ranged from 45% to 100%, and specificity ranged from 10% to 99%. The pooled sensitivity of chest CT was 86.9% (95% confidence interval [CI]: 83.6% to 89.6%), and the pooled specificity was 78.3% (95% CI: 73.7% to 82.3%). Sensitivity was influenced by the definition of test positivity, but specificity was not. For chest X-ray (17 studies, 8,529 participants, 62% confirmed cases), sensitivity ranged from 44% to 94%, and specificity ranged from 24% to 93%. The pooled sensitivity was 73.1% (95% CI: 64.1% to 80.5%), and the pooled specificity was 73.3% (95% CI: 61.9% to 82.2%). No significant sources of heterogeneity were identified for chest X-ray. For lung ultrasound (15 studies, 2,410 participants, 48% confirmed cases), sensitivity ranged from 73% to 94%, and specificity ranged from 21% to 98%. The pooled sensitivity was 88.9% (95% CI: 84.9% to 92.0%), and the pooled specificity was 72.2% (95% CI: 58.8% to 82.5%). No significant sources of heterogeneity were identified for lung ultrasound. Indirect comparisons across all 94 studies revealed that chest CT and ultrasound had higher sensitivity than chest X-ray (P = 0.0003 and P = 0.001, respectively). However, chest CT and ultrasound had similar sensitivities (P = 0.42). Specificities were comparable across all modalities. For individuals with initially negative RT-PCR results who later tested positive, 8 studies (7 CT, 1 ultrasound) involving 198 participants were included. Among 177 participants with initially negative RT-PCR results who later tested positive, 75.8% (95% CI: 45.3% to 92.2%) had positive CT findings. For asymptomatic individuals, 10 studies (7 CT, 1 X-ray, 2 ultrasound) involving 3,548 participants were included. Of these, 364 participants (10%) were ultimately diagnosed with COVID-19. For chest CT (7 studies, 3,134 participants, 10% confirmed cases), the pooled sensitivity was 55.7% (95% CI: 35.4% to 74.3%), and the pooled specificity was 91.1% (95% CI: 82.6% to 95.7%). In conclusion, chest CT and lung ultrasound are highly sensitive and moderately specific for diagnosing COVID-19, while chest X-ray is moderately sensitive and specific. Chest CT and ultrasound may be more effective for ruling out COVID-19 rather than distinguishing SARS-CoV-2 infection from other respiratory illnesses. However, the high or unclear risk of bias and heterogeneity across studies limit the strength of these conclusions.
